caption:
Wizards of the Coast, the company behind Dungeons & Dragons, is giving up its share of the Anthropic AI copyright settlement.
The money goes to the writers of its D&D novels, modules and stories instead.
One author says it adds up to hundreds of thousands of dollars.

Should every publisher hand its AI settlement money to the writers?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: Wargamer, PC Gamer · Photo: Wizards of the Coast
threads_text: The company behind Dungeons & Dragons is giving its whole share of the Anthropic AI copyright settlement to the writers of its books. Normally the publisher keeps half. Should every publisher do the same?

slides.headline: D&D's owner is handing its *entire Anthropic payout* to writers

slides.heading: Pirated books, *real money*
paras: Anthropic agreed to a $1.5 billion settlement with authors whose books were pirated to train its AI. A judge approved it in July 2026.
Each eligible book gets at least $3,000, normally split 50/50 between publisher and author.

slides.heading: Wizards gives up *its half*
paras: Wizards of the Coast filed claims as the copyright owner of its D&D novels, modules and stories.
Now it says it will pass its share to the authors who wrote them. Letters telling writers how to claim went out this week.

slides.heading: *Hundreds of thousands* of dollars
paras: Forgotten Realms author James Lowder broke the news. He says the money WotC could have kept amounts to hundreds of thousands of dollars.

paras.t: He credited Wizards head Dan Ayoub and author R.A. Salvatore.

slides.hook: Follow to see who gets paid next as the AI copyright fights play out.

paragraphs.text: Wizards of the Coast, the publisher of Dungeons & Dragons, will give its share of the Bartz v. Anthropic copyright settlement to the authors of its D&D novels, modules and stories, according to Wargamer, PC Gamer and EN World. Wargamer published a statement from the company on November 20, 2026.

The news first came from James Lowder, a freelance writer and editor who has written Forgotten Realms and Ravenloft novels for the game. In a post reported by Wargamer and PC Gamer, Lowder wrote that Wizards of the Coast was forgoing its share of the payout and giving all of the money to the authors.

The settlement resolves a class action brought by authors whose books were pirated and used in the development of Anthropic's AI models. Wargamer and PC Gamer put its size at $1.5 billion. Wargamer reported that the deal was agreed in September 2025 and approved by a judge in July 2026, and that around 500,000 books were eligible.

Each eligible book is paid at least $3,000, minus fees, according to Wargamer. The money is shared among the rightsholders of each work, and the default split gives half to the publisher and half to the author, although authors can agree a different share with their publisher.

EN World gave a different total for the settlement, $1.3 billion, and said the central library of pirated material contained more than 7 million books. The outlet also noted that some separate lawsuits brought by authors are still ongoing.
What Wizards of the Coast said

In its statement, Wizards of the Coast said it took part in the settlement as the copyright owner of Dungeons & Dragons novels, modules and stories, and that it plans to share its portion of the payments with the authors of those works. EN World attributed the statement to Blain Howard, senior manager of brand publicity for D&D. The company also said that authors had begun receiving letters that week explaining how to claim their share.

A letter quoted by Lowder explained that Wizards of the Coast filed the claims in its own name because it is the registered owner of the works. Lowder estimated that the money the company is giving up amounts to hundreds of thousands of dollars. He credited Wizards of the Coast staff, in particular company head Dan Ayoub, for being open to the discussions, and said author R.A. Salvatore's efforts helped start them.

Neither the company nor the outlets said how many Wizards of the Coast titles are covered or how much each author will receive. EN World reported that the exact number of authors who will be paid is not yet known.

For many writers of licensed game fiction and adventure modules, the publisher owns the copyright, which means the settlement checks would normally go first to the company. The decision by Wizards of the Coast shows how much the outcome of AI copyright settlements for individual writers can depend on choices made by their publishers rather than by the AI company that pays.
Other publishers that registered copyrights for work written by freelancers face the same choice about their half of the Anthropic payments, and authors are now receiving claim letters.
